analysis.one_liner: Lets federal regulators ban repeat energy market manipulators from trading electricity and natural gas.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where no further action has been taken; it has one sponsor and 12 cosponsors, all Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill gives the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission new tools against energy market manipulation. It would let the agency temporarily or permanently bar any person or company from trading electricity or natural gas if they manipulate those markets or file false price information with the government or private price-reporting agencies. It also makes it a specific violation to knowingly file false natural gas price data. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and has seen no action since.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses that pay electricity and natural gas bills. Manipulation in wholesale energy markets — like the schemes that drove California's electricity crisis in 2000-01 and the Enron-era price games — ultimately shows up in consumer bills. By letting regulators ban bad actors from the markets entirely, the bill aims to deter manipulation at the source rather than just issuing fines that companies can treat as a cost of doing business.

how_it_helps.text: Allows FERC to prohibit, conditionally or unconditionally, permanently or temporarily, any person found to have violated market manipulation rules from directly or indirectly purchasing or selling electric energy, electricity products (including financial transmission rights), or transmission services.
Extends the same ban authority to natural gas markets, covering anyone who violated gas price-reporting rules.

Creates a new prohibition under the Natural Gas Act on willfully and knowingly filing false information with federal agencies or private price-reporting agencies about natural gas transportation, availability, or wholesale prices, with intent to fraudulently affect the data.

Expands the scope of enforcement from 'individuals' to any 'person' acting directly or indirectly, closing a gap that let firms manipulate markets through traders or subsidiaries without their entity being barred.

analysis.who_pays: Energy trading firms, wholesale power and gas marketers, and the parent companies behind them, who would face the real possibility of being barred from lucrative markets for manipulation or false price reports. Honest market participants bear little direct cost, though regulated entities could face broader penalty exposure.
analysis.who_pays_short: Energy trading firms and wholesale marketers

drawbacks.text: The ban power is discretionary and the standard is a violation of existing manipulation provisions, so its real effect depends on how aggressively FERC enforces it; skeptics could argue it adds penalties where existing civil fines and disgorgement already exist.

Broad language barring 'any person' acting 'directly or indirectly' from trading could sweep in affiliates and counterparties beyond the manipulator itself, raising due-process and fairness questions that a committee would need to refine.
Tighter enforcement of wholesale price reporting could add compliance costs for gas shippers and traders, which some would pass on in market prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — a credible deterrent against price manipulation in markets that set household energy bills — is real but modest in scale, since it strengthens existing enforcement rather than creating a new price control. The main costs are compliance and possible overreach in barring affiliates. On balance, the consumer benefit outweighs the costs, but the bill is narrow enough that its practical impact depends entirely on enforcement.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor action; Congress is still in session, so it is technically alive but dormant.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on April 21, 2026, joined by 12 cosponsors, all Democrats.
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce.
No further action — no committee hearing, no markup, no vote — appears in the action history since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, energy trading firms and wholesale power and gas marketers are better off: a bill to bar manipulators from trading has stalled in committee, and the status quo of fines-only enforcement continues.

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 12 Democratic cosponsors to expand FERC's power to ban energy market manipulators.

for.name: Reps. Beyer, Casten, Moulton, Jayapal, Huffman, Kelly (IL), Quigley, Norton, Castor (FL), Case, Goldman (NY), and Lofgren
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors the day of introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no further action — no hearing or markup — leaving it dormant.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats, with no Republican support on record, and the committee of referral has not acted.

industries.industry: Energy trading firms and wholesale electricity/gas marketers
industries.note: The bill lets FERC permanently or temporarily bar manipulators and false price reporters from trading electricity, gas, and related products — turning a fine into a potential business-ending penalty. Consumers pay wholesale-driven retail bills, so enforcement against manipulators runs with the public interest rather than against it.

The bill covers transmission services under FERC jurisdiction, so legitimate utilities face some new enforcement exposure, but cleaner wholesale markets reduce the manipulation-driven price spikes that utilities have historically had to pass through to customers.
False reports to private price-reporting agencies become a named violation, which raises the stakes for the accuracy of the data those agencies rely on but adds no direct regulatory burden on them.

analysis.trajectory: With no committee action since its April 2026 referral, no Republican cosponsors, and a crowded agenda in Energy and Commerce, the bill is likely to die quietly at the end of the 119th Congress unless a related energy enforcement vehicle picks up its provisions.
